overview: The atlas alternates two broad labels: “Rajput kingdoms” in 1000 to 1100 and 1200 to 1279, and “Hindu kingdoms” in 1100 to 1200. This shared page covers regional ruling networks, not one empire or everyone’s religion. The middle outline covers the northwest; the later one misleadingly reaches southern India. These are unreliable borders. Examples complement separate dynasty cards; Bhojpur and Chandravati lie outside the middle-century outline.

periods.title: First Rajput snapshot
periods.summary: The atlas groups regional powers under a broad outline.

periods.title: The Hindu kingdoms label
periods.summary: The map switches to a northwestern umbrella.

periods.title: Rajput label returns
periods.summary: The later outline extends far beyond these regional states.

items.text: Forts anchored control over surrounding farmland as well as military defence. IGNOU’s historical survey connects regional strongholds with rural property and landed authority. A king needed food and people behind the walls, and connections beyond them.

Marriage between ruling clans helped create political alliances and social standing. Rajput identity developed through changing relationships among families, warriors and landholders; it was not a single unchanged ancestry shared by everyone living in these territories.

At Kiradu in 1161, Somesvara’s praise inscription placed a local Paramara ruler within the power of the Chaulukya king Kumarapala. Such records reveal layered authority: an ambitious regional lord could advertise victories while acknowledging a more powerful king.

An early twelfth-century Jalor inscription credits Queen Melaradevi, wife of Visala, with furnishing a Shiva temple with a golden cupola. Royal women could commission highly visible religious gifts in their own names. This is one queen’s documented patronage, not a description of every woman’s opportunities.

sections.title: A giant building site left unfinished

items.text: At Bhojpur, the eleventh-century Paramara king Bhoja is associated with an enormous Shiva temple that was never completed. Its surviving hall has four columns about 12 metres tall. The unfinished structure lets researchers investigate decisions that a completed building might have hidden.

Builders scratched architectural drawings onto the surrounding rock: plans, pillars, doorways, capitals and measurements for spacing columns. These were working aids at the construction site. Imagine doing your geometry homework on the ground, then using the answer to position a giant stone pillar.

Carved blocks still lie around Bhojpur, and surviving earthen ramps help explain how heavy building materials could be raised. Nearby dam remains show that the project also reshaped the Betwa river landscape. ASI excavations in 1950 investigated the temple area, adding excavation evidence to the visible ruins.

sections.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers

items.text: Excavations at Chandravati from 2013 to 2016 uncovered remains of a town with substantial religious buildings. Researchers describe temple platforms built in brick and the use of marble from the Ambaji area. Stone arriving from a quarry had to pass through the hands of transport workers, builders and sculptors.

A Chandravati panel dated to the twelfth or thirteenth century shows worshippers queued before a Jain image. The excavators interpret objects in their hands as possible water pots for ritual bathing of the image. Even a carved medieval crowd seems familiar: everyone waiting for a turn.

Another sculpture of the same broad period shows a woman adjusting her anklet. Religious art could include recognizable gestures of dressing and adornment. This little action gives a more personal glimpse than a list of royal victories, although an idealized sculpture is not a household photograph.

Charred crop remains from Chandravati’s roughly 800 to 1300 phase include barley and rice; the researchers also illustrate wheat from that phase. Winter and summer crops both appear. These are actual traces of the plant economy, though surviving seeds cannot tell us precisely what every family ate for dinner.

Researchers dated charred grain, seeds and wood, then compared the town’s evidence with pollen from nearby Mandovari Lake. They interpret the diverse medieval crops alongside relatively favourable monsoon conditions. Burnt food can be a disaster for a cook and a useful clue for an archaeologist.

A twelfth-century Sarasvati from Pallu, now in the National Museum, stands about 77 centimetres high and carries symbols including a book and rosary. The museum identifies her as the Jain goddess of learning. Books mattered in this religious imagery, but the statue cannot tell us how many children attended lessons.

Kiradu’s Sanskrit inscription says “प्रशस्तिमकरोदेतां”, here rendered in modern Devanagari from the scholarly transcription praśastim akarod etāṃ: “composed this eulogy”. The next words name Narasimha acting at the king’s order. These are words from a specific 1161 court monument, not a sample of everyone’s everyday speech.

The Kiradu record survives on a temple pillar and has been studied through impressions and successive editions. Some letters have been lost or damaged. The modern edition marks restored passages with brackets; the short sample above avoids those restorations.

sections.title: What continued after the atlas label

items.text: Later Rajasthan forts enclosed temples, homes, markets and palaces, with water-harvesting systems that helped sustain these communities. Jaisalmer remains inhabited. These buildings developed over many centuries, so its present-day streets and reservoirs should not all be assigned to the map’s 1000 to 1279 interval.

Chandravati’s excavations show occupation continuing into the late seventeenth century. Its eventual decline was much later than this atlas cutoff. The study considers environmental stress alongside historical and institutional changes, rather than giving every settlement in the region one shared disaster story.

ending.text: There was no collective collapse in 1200 or 1279, the endpoints of these imported labels. Regional dynasties faced different wars, successions and changing alliances, while Rajput courts and communities continued for centuries. Rajasthan’s surviving fort traditions extend into the eighteenth century and include later interactions with Sultanate and Mughal architecture.
